transcript:
MEETING HEADER
Date: 2026-06-10
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Park (Redwood AE), Ravi Menon (Redwood SE), Elena Ruiz (Redwood Infra), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Marcus Hale (Luminex CTO), Priya Anand (Luminex ML), Tomás Reyes (Luminex Infra), Leah Kim (Luminex Security), Wei Zhou (Perf Eng)

AUTO SUMMARY (auto-gen, brief): Demo of multi-stage chunking for extremely long contexts; benchmarks discussed; plan for on-prem 256k test.

--- TRANSCRIPT ---
[00:00] Sophie Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, small intro from our side. I'm Sophie, AE. Ravi and Elena here are gonna drive the technical bits. Marcus, do you want to kick off with what you're trying to solve?
[00:18] Marcus Hale: Yeah thanks, Sophie. High level, two use-cases: 1) long-form legal document ingest where users need full 6-8 hour session state, so contexts 100k+ tokens, and 2) cross-document search + synthesis where we want the model to reason over 256k token-ish window. Our main asks: predictable latency (p95 under 1s for short interactions), and ability to do batch offline synthesis.
[00:42] Priya Anand: Also to add, we can't ship all raw docs off-prem for compliance, so we'll likely need private deployment in our VPC and key management. We want to understand memory tradeoffs and whether we can use caching of embeddings + KV to reduce cost.
[01:05] Ravi Menon: Great. We'll focus today on architecture patterns: chunking strategies (sliding, hierarchical, sparse attention routing), KV cache policies (sharding, TTL, on-disk spill), and quantization impacts on kernel selection and throughput. We'll try to keep it practical.
[01:25] Tomás Reyes: Quick infra note: our test bed will be H100s but we're also trying to estimate A100 baselines. Network between nodes is 100GbE, and the VPC will be peered to Redwood private control plane for management. Security's strict — Leah will chime in for KMS/HSM requirements.
[01:45] Leah Kim: Yes, we need HSM-backed keys and full audit logs; any on-prem Redwood agent must run without exfiltration and support SAML SSO.
[02:05] Sophie Park: Noted. Okay Ravi, take us through chunking.
[02:12] Ravi Menon: Start with the simplest: sliding window with overlap. Works fine up to maybe 32k where the KV cache still fits in memory, but is inefficient at 100k+ because you reencode overlapping tokens repeatedly. So second pattern is hierarchical chunking: break docs into small chunks, compute chunk-level embeddings and summaries, then a top-level attention over chunk summaries. That reduces cross-chunk KV size.
[02:45] Marcus Hale: But hierarchical introduces approximation — do we lose important cross-sentence context?
[02:50] Ravi Menon: Yes tradeoff. We use hybrid approach: preserve a small prefix KV for the most recent N tokens with full attention, and use chunk summaries for distant context. For critical sections we maintain a bloom-filter index to rehydrate original tokens on demand. There's overhead but it's rare paths.
[03:14] Priya Anand: Can you sketch the cache eviction? If we keep prefix KV in memory, how do we evict older kvs while ensuring coherent replies?
[03:25] Elena Ruiz: Typical policy is LRU with segment weights by recency and relevance score from embedding. For long sessions, we tier: hot in-GPU KV, warm in host RAM with fast on-disk spill (nvme), cold archived. If an inference needs cold data, we fetch and stitch — latency hit but bounded.
[03:49] Wei Zhou: Do you stripe KV across GPUs for 256k? Concerned about all-gather costs.
[03:56] Ravi Menon: Good point. Two strategies: model-parallel KV sharding where each GPU holds a contiguous slice of the KV for faster local access but requires cross-GPU gather for attention; or replicated KV where we duplicate hot KV across GPUs to avoid all-gather but at memory cost. For 256k, replication is often infeasible unless you quantize aggressively.
[04:21] Tomás Reyes: On replication: how much memory reduction do we get with 4-bit quant vs 8-bit?
[04:28] Daniel Cho: In practice, GPTQ-style 4-bit with per-channel scales can reduce KV footprint ~2x-4x compared to 16-bit, but you pay CPU/GPU cycles to dequantize and the throughput depends on whether kernels are optimized. On H100 we can use tensor cores well with bf16/8-bit kernels, but custom 4-bit pathways require Triton or fused kernels to avoid a big perf hit.
[04:55] Marcus Hale: So for our H100 cluster we'd likely see replication feasible at 32k but not 256k unless quantized.
[05:03] Ravi Menon: Exactly. And there's a third approach: sparse attention patterns — local window for most tokens + global tokens for routeing (think BigBird/Longformer). Using routing attention or clustered attention reduces kv length in practice. We showed a routing-attention prototype that keeps complexity near-linear.
[05:26] Priya Anand: How deterministic is routing attention? We need reproducible outputs for audits.
[05:33] Ravi Menon: Routing introduces non-determinism unless you pin seeds; determinism is achievable but be careful with top-k routing thresholds. For audited pipelines, we recommend a deterministic routing mode and recording routing indices in logs for replay.
[05:51] Leah Kim: Recording routing indices is fine but that may reveal secret structure — is there an encryption concern?
[05:58] Elena Ruiz: We treat routing metadata as pseudonymized telemetry; for sensitive setups we store it in the customer's KMS-protected store and redact externally.
[06:12] Sophie Park: Let's talk throughput: continuous batching vs single-request low latency.
[06:18] Ravi Menon: Continuous batching pools inflight requests for a short window (e.g., 10-50ms) to form large token batches and improve GPU utilization. Great for throughput-intensive workloads, but does add tail latency variability. For p95 latency-sensitive UIs, we use a hybrid: small dynamic batching with priority preemption for interactive traffic and larger background batches for offline synthesis.
[06:42] Wei Zhou: What about KV cache warm-up when using batching? If different requests want different prefixes, can cache reuse still help?
[06:52] Daniel Cho: Yes, prefix caching and common-prefix detection are crucial. Use a suffix-tree or hash-based prefix matcher to find shared KV segments; batch requests with common prefixes together. It reduces duplicated attention compute.
[07:09] Marcus Hale: How does on-disk spill affect latency in VPC? Our NVMe is local but across nodes it's slower.
[07:17] Elena Ruiz: If you spill to local NVMe it's reasonably fast (few ms). Cross-node calls depend on fabric: RDMA or GPUDirect can help. But we try to avoid cross-node spills by placing responsible shards local to request routing layer. That ties into smart routing policies in Redwood — route to node that already has the hot KV when possible.
[07:39] Priya Anand: We want to test checkpointing: if we snapshot KV to disk periodically, can we warm up faster later?
[07:47] Ravi Menon: Yes, snapshot-and-warm is a recommended pattern. Create lightweight serialized KV segments and a manifest. For very long sessions, incremental snapshots every N tokens keep restore time bounded.
[07:58] Sophie Park: On quantization and kernel selection — Daniel walk us through the tradeoffs when we move to 4-bit.
[08:04] Daniel Cho: With 4-bit you save memory, but naive dequantize/compute pipeline burns cycles. Best path is fused 4-bit matmul kernels that operate on compressed representation. There are open-source GPTQ kernels and vendor-optimized triton kernels; H100 favors bf16/FP16 pipelines so you see the highest throughput with 8-bit/bf16 unless the fused 4-bit kernel is mature. Also watch accuracy degradation—some sensitive tasks need per-channel vs per-tensor scales.
[08:34] Marcus Hale: Any benchmark numbers you can share from Redwood?
[08:38] Ravi Menon: High-level: on H100 a baseline bfloat16 70B model at 32k context does X tokens/sec (we'll attach spreadsheet). With GPTQ 4-bit we saw 1.8-2.6x reduction in memory footprint and typically 1.1-1.8x improvements in effective throughput depending on kernel maturity. But for 256k contexts the memory pressure dominates and quantization enables feasibility more than speed-ups alone.
[09:03] Priya Anand: For our compliance use-case, we favored deterministic outputs. How much does quantization affect determinism?
[09:10] Daniel Cho: Quantization affects numerical results but deterministic execution is still possible; the model outputs will differ slightly but will be reproducible given the same quantized weights and same kernel path. When exact float equivalence is required, quantization is not acceptable.
[09:25] Tomás Reyes: Let's talk about model partitioning. Do you shard KV across sequence dimension or head dimension?
[09:32] Ravi Menon: Options: sequence-shard (each GPU stores contiguous sequence ranges) vs head-shard (shard attention heads). Sequence-shard is friendly to KV locality for long contexts but requires an all-reduce for softmax results. Head-shard splits compute differently. There's also a pipeline-hybrid where you combine model parallelism with tensor slicing to fit memory. For 256k contexts, sequence-aware sharding plus compressed KV is common.
[09:58] Wei Zhou: How about recomputation vs storing KV? If we recompute past activations we trade compute for memory.
[10:05] Daniel Cho: Yes, recompute can reduce memory footprint at the cost of extra FLOPs. For very large contexts, recompute selective layers or use reversible layers to lower memory at moderate compute cost. Many opt for a mixed strategy: keep keys/values for the last N tokens, recompute earlier activations.
[10:28] Marcus Hale: Any thoughts on attention approximations like Nyströmformer or Performer?
[10:34] Ravi Menon: They help in some cases. Nyström/Performer reduce complexity but can degrade accuracy on fine-grained reasoning. We recommend them for initial scaling experiments, but for legal/finance where fidelity is critical, hierarchical + routing attention tends to be safer.
[10:52] Priya Anand: On encryption: if KV sits in host RAM or NVMe, does Redwood encrypt at rest in the Private offering?
[10:59] Elena Ruiz: Yes — disk encryption, and RAM-level encryption is supported via AMD SEV/Intel TDX in certain configurations. All keys are KMS/HSM-backed, and audit logs record key use. For air-gapped on-prem we can integrate with customer HSMs.
[11:15] Leah Kim: How about telemetry — we need to ensure only aggregated perf metrics are sent back.
[11:21] Sophie Park: We support opt-out and can restrict telemetry to anonymized performance counters; for enterprise we do an explicit data sharing agreement.
[11:30] Marcus Hale: Back to batching: any suggestions for scheduling in a mixed workload (interactive + bulk)?
[11:36] Ravi Menon: Use priority queues with deadline-aware scheduler, plus dynamic batch sizing. Assign tickets for interactive, preempt larger batches if an interactive request arrives. Also assign token budgets per request to limit runaway long-token requests.
[11:52] Tomás Reyes: Are there open-source tools you recommend for measuring memory vs compute tradeoffs?
[11:57] Daniel Cho: We often use perf counters, Nsight for GPU, and a custom Redwood harness that simulates long token sequences and reports per-layer mem & time. We'll share the harness as a runnable container.
[12:12] Priya Anand: About modeling changes — does it make sense to finetune a model for sparse attention patterns?
[12:18] Ravi Menon: Yes, models trained with sparse attention primitives or with retrieval-aware objectives are more robust when you later apply routing. Fine-tuning on long contexts with controlled negatives can help retain reasoning quality when you compress context.
[12:33] Marcus Hale: Let's get practical — what would Redwood recommend as a minimum test to validate 256k viability?
[12:38] Sophie Park: Good question. Our recommended test plan: a) baseline run with full context build using 16-bit on H100 for a scaled-down 100k run, b) run with GPTQ 4-bit kernels to measure memory headroom, c) hierarchical chunking + routing mode run to measure quality delta, and d) an end-to-end on-prem 256k run. We'll provide configs.
[12:58] Wei Zhou: Want to see latency numbers for 1, 8, 32 concurrent sessions at 256k.
[13:04] Ravi Menon: We'll include concurrency curves. Expect tail latency growth; the chart will show batching benefits past a concurrency threshold.
[13:13] Priya Anand: Any gotchas in the Redwood Private agent during air-gapped runs?
[13:18] Elena Ruiz: Biggest is initial artifact provisioning—models and kernels must be staged. Also, some triton kernels may require vendor drivers; we work with your infra to stage them. Our private control plane can operate in offline mode for orchestration.
[13:33] Marcus Hale: Security question: can Redwood's rollout and tracing hooks be disabled?
[13:38] Sophie Park: Yes — for private/on-prem customers we can disable remote tracing and only provide local logs; config flags exist.
[13:44] Leah Kim: Would like to see RBAC mapping for infra engineers vs app owners.
[13:49] Daniel Cho: We'll send RBAC doc and a template mapping.
[13:53] Tomás Reyes: About cost: does Redwood have unit economics for token costs with big contexts?
[13:59] Sophie Park: Cost per token changes with batching, KV reuse, and quantization. Redwood Optimize can simulate and give estimated $/1000 tokens for your workload; we'll run your workload profile through it.
[14:12] Priya Anand: Can we get a drill-down into the exact kernel versions you use? We may need to reproduce bugs.
[14:18] Ravi Menon: We'll share kernel manifest (Triton versions, fused kernels, and any patches). For reproducibility we also include docker hashes.
[14:29] Wei Zhou: On the topic of model fallbacks — if memory blows up can Redwood auto-fallback to a smaller context model?
[14:36] Elena Ruiz: Yes, Redwood has runtime policies: cap tokens, fall back to reduced context variant, or serve degraded mode with summary-only context. The policy is configurable per-route.
[14:50] Marcus Hale: Performance regression monitoring is important — how do we detect quality regressions due to quantization?
[14:56] Ravi Menon: Tie prompt sets and reference outputs into eval hooks. Redwood Optimize can run nightly/every-deploy checks and alert on quality metrics. We'll link your legal prompt set to the eval pipeline.
[15:09] Priya Anand: For the on-prem run, who will own the benchmark execution?
[15:13] Sophie Park: Redwood SEs will run jointly with Luminex infra; we'll do a dry-run, then a measured run.
[15:19] Marcus Hale: Can you write that in the action items?
[15:22] Sophie Park: Yes, added — see action items.
[15:25] (crosstalk)
[15:30] Daniel Cho: Quick note on profiler data — collecting per-layer timings at 256k can be noisy; suggest repeated runs with warm-up iterations and median aggregation.
[15:43] Wei Zhou: Any pointer about disk-backed KV formats? Columnar? Flatbuffers?
[15:48] Elena Ruiz: We use compact binary manifests (flatbuffers) and chunked compressed segments (snappy or zstd) optimized for streaming decompress on GPU.
[16:00] Marcus Hale: What about dev tools — how do we debug long-context misalignments?
[16:05] Ravi Menon: Redwood Console exposes token-level traces, attention heatmaps (sampling, not full due to volume), and a rehydration trace to show which chunk summaries were used. We can toggle more verbose traces in private installs.
[16:22] Priya Anand: Any regulatory red flags when storing partial KV or embeddings? For us embeddings are PII-ish.
[16:29] Leah Kim: We will need clear guidance: treat embeddings as sensitive, encrypt, and set TTL.
[16:35] Elena Ruiz: Agreed — we recommend encryption at rest + short TTL for embeddings and advisory for anonymization.
[16:45] Sophie Park: We're nearing the end — let's recap and confirm next steps.
[16:50] Marcus Hale: Recap: Redwood will share configs/benchmarks and kernel manifest; we'll stand up H100 cluster and collect baseline metrics; schedule joint on-prem run. Security team will validate KMS/HSM integration.
[17:05] Sophie Park: Action items and owners posted. We'll email the packet and set up a 2-hour slot next week for the full benchmark. Any final quick questions?
[17:15] Priya Anand: No, thanks, this was great.
[17:18] Marcus Hale: Appreciate it.
[17:20] Sophie Park: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts.

END TRANSCRIPT
